title: TypeScript, the type-level parts
blurb: Conditional and mapped types, inference, overloads, module settings and the soundness holes: what a senior reviewer expects you to read fluently even if you rarely write it.

questions.q: Which call fails to compile, and why?
choices: `len('abc')`, because a string primitive is not an object with properties
Neither, because T is inferred from each argument and so always satisfies it
`len(42)`, because `number` has no `length` property to meet the constraint
Both, because a constrained generic needs an explicit type argument
questions.why: `extends { length: number }` limits T to types with a numeric `length`. Strings qualify, because primitives are checked through their wrapper type's members. Inference picks T from the argument, but the inferred T must still satisfy the constraint, so 42 is rejected.
questions.asked: Constraints are the first thing that separates a useful generic from `any` with angle brackets.

questions.code:
type ApiResponse<T = unknown> = { data: T; status: number };
const r: ApiResponse = { data: 42, status: 200 };
choices: `number`, inferred from the value 42 that is assigned to it
`unknown`, because the omitted argument takes the default
`any`, because no type argument was supplied at all
A compile error: `ApiResponse` needs one type argument
questions.why: A default makes the type argument optional, and an annotation that omits it gets the default. A type in an annotation is never inferred from the initialiser, so it is not `number`; and without `= unknown` the line would be a 'requires 1 type argument' error.
questions.asked: Defaults are all over library signatures, and reading them tells you what you get when you leave the angle brackets off.

questions.q: What does tsc report for the call to `pair`?
choices: Nothing; T is widened to the union `string | number` to fit both of the arguments
Nothing; T is inferred as `unknown` because the arguments disagree
An error on `1`: number is not assignable to a parameter of type string
An error on `'one'`: string is not assignable to a parameter of type number
questions.why: With several candidates for T, inference looks for a best common type rather than building a union; `number` and `string` have none, so T is fixed from the first candidate and `'one'` is rejected. Write `pair<string | number>(1, 'one')` if a union is what you want.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know inference is a heuristic with rules, not a solver that finds any type that works.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.0+, what is the type of `r`?
choices: `readonly ['admin', 'editor']`
`['admin', 'editor']`
`('admin' | 'editor')[]`
`readonly ('admin' | 'editor')[]`
questions.why: A `const` type parameter makes inference treat the argument as if the caller had written `as const`, so the literals and the tuple shape survive, and the readonly constraint lets the readonly tuple fit. Without the modifier, T is inferred as plain `string[]`.
questions.asked: Router and schema libraries use it to get literal types without making every caller type `as const`.

questions.code:
type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never;
type A = ToArray<string | number>;
choices: `(string | number)[]`
`[string, number]`
`string[] | number[]`
`string[] & number[]`
questions.why: A conditional type whose checked type is a bare type parameter distributes over a union: it runs once per member and unions the results. So each member gets its own array type rather than one mixed array, which is what `(string | number)[]` would be.
questions.asked: Distribution explains most "why did my utility type produce this?" surprises, and it is how Exclude and Extract work under the hood.

choices: `[number, string]`
`number`
`(id: number) => void`
`unknown`
questions.why: `infer A` declares a type variable that the compiler fills in by matching F against the pattern, so A captures the first parameter's type. `[number, string]` is what you get by inferring the whole parameter list, which is how the built-in `Parameters` is written.
questions.asked: Reading `infer` fluently is what a reviewer needs for library types; writing a small one is the usual follow-up.

questions.code:
type IsString<T> = [T] extends [string] ? true : false;
type A = IsString<'a' | 1>;
choices: `boolean`
`true`
`never`
`false`
questions.why: Wrapping T in a one-element tuple means the checked type is no longer a naked type parameter, so the union is tested as a whole, and `'a' | 1` is not assignable to string. Without the brackets it would distribute into `true | false`, which is `boolean`.
questions.asked: The bracket trick is the standard answer to "my conditional type behaves oddly with unions".

questions.code:
type IsNever<T> = T extends never ? true : false;
type A = IsNever<never>;
choices: `true`
`false`
`never`
`boolean`
questions.why: `never` is the empty union, and a distributive conditional runs once per member, so with no members the result is never; write `[T] extends [never]` to test it. The same rule is why never vanishes from unions: `string | never` is just `string`.
questions.asked: It looks like trivia, but it is the root cause of utility types that silently return never.

choices: `{ getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }`
`{ name: () => string; age: () => number }`
`{ getName: string; getAge: number }`
`{ getName: () => unknown; getAge: () => unknown }`
questions.why: The `as` clause renames each key while `T[K]` still indexes with the original key, so the value types survive the rename. `string & K` is needed because `keyof T` can include number and symbol keys, which `Capitalize` does not accept.
questions.asked: Key remapping is how libraries derive handler and getter names, and reviewers meet it in form and store typings.

questions.code:
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type M = Mutable<{ readonly id: number }>;
choices: `{ readonly id: number }`, since modifiers cannot be removed
`{ id?: number }`, since the `-` prefix marks it optional
A compile error, since `readonly` is fixed where declared
`{ id: number }`, since `-readonly` strips the modifier
questions.why: Mapped types can add (`+`, the default) or remove (`-`) the `readonly` and `?` modifiers; `-?` is how `Required<T>` is written. The removal is shallow: a nested readonly array stays readonly.
questions.asked: A quick check that you can read modifier syntax in library types rather than skipping over it.

questions.q: Which statement about `A` and `B` is true?
choices: `A` and `B` both keep `note` optional, as its property type is identical
`A` keeps `note` optional; in `B` it is required but may be undefined
`A` and `B` both make `note` required, as mapped types drop modifiers
`B` keeps `note` optional; `A` makes every property required
questions.why: A mapped type over `keyof T` is homomorphic: the compiler knows each key came from T and copies its `?` and `readonly` modifiers. Mapping over a literal key union has no source object, so `note` becomes a required `string | undefined` and `{ id: 1 }` no longer fits B.
questions.asked: It explains why `Pick` preserves optionality while a `Record` over the same keys does not.

questions.q: Which type for per-field error messages rejects misspelt field names but lets a valid field have no error?
questions.code: type User = { email: string; age: number };
choices: `Record<string, string | undefined>`
`{ [K in keyof User]: string }`
`{ [K in keyof User]?: string }`
`{ [K in keyof User]?: User[K] }`
questions.why: Mapping over `keyof User` keeps the errors type in step with the model, and `?` lets a field have no entry. `Record<string, string>` accepts `emial`, the non-optional mapping demands a message for every field, and `?: User[K]` (which is `Partial<User>`) keeps the field types, so an age message would have to be a number.
questions.asked: Deriving form state from the model is the most common place a mid-level developer writes a mapped type.

questions.code:
const handlers = { create() {}, remove() {} };
type Action = keyof typeof handlers;
choices: `'create' | 'remove'`
`string`
`{ create(): void; remove(): void }`
`('create' | 'remove')[]`
questions.why: `typeof` in a type position turns a value into its type, and `keyof` then gives the union of its keys. Writing `keyof handlers` on its own is an error, because `handlers` is a value, not a type.
questions.asked: Deriving a union from a runtime object keeps one source of truth, and interviewers want to see you reach for it.

questions.code:
const users = [{ id: 1, name: 'Ann' }, { id: 2, name: 'Bo' }];
type User = (typeof users)[number];
choices: `{ id: number; name: string }[]`
`number`
`{ id: 1; name: 'Ann' } | { id: 2; name: 'Bo' }`
`{ id: number; name: string }`
questions.why: Indexing an array type with `number` gives its element type, because any numeric index yields an element. The literals are widened because the array and its objects are mutable; only `as const` would keep them.
questions.asked: It is the everyday way to name the element type of data you already have, such as fixtures or a config list.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.4+, what happens on the last line?
questions.code:
function pickSize<T extends string>(options: T[], initial: NoInfer<T>) {}
pickSize(['sm', 'md'], 'xl');
choices: It compiles, and T is inferred as `'sm' | 'md' | 'xl'`
An error: `'xl'` is not assignable to `'sm' | 'md'`
It compiles, and T is widened to `string` by `'xl'`
An error: `NoInfer` cannot wrap a constrained type parameter
questions.why: `NoInfer<T>` stops that position from contributing inference candidates, so T comes only from `options` and `'xl'` is then checked against it. Without it both arguments are candidates and T silently becomes `'sm' | 'md' | 'xl'`, the bug the helper exists to prevent.
questions.asked: It shows you know which arguments drive inference, the question behind most "why did this generic accept that?" bugs.

questions.q: What does tsc report on the last line?
choices: An error: no overload matches a `string | number` argument
Nothing; the implementation signature accepts the union
Nothing; the call resolves to a return type of `number | string`
An error: the implementation's return type is not annotated
questions.why: Callers see only the overload signatures, each tried on its own, and a `string | number` argument fits neither. The implementation signature is invisible from outside, so it does not rescue the call. Add a union overload, or use one signature with a conditional return type.
questions.asked: The follow-up is "overloads or a union parameter?", and the usual answer is the union unless the return type depends on the input.

questions.q: What is the type of `el` on the last line?
choices: `HTMLElement | null`, because the call result is never checked
`never`, because the function may throw before returning
`HTMLElement`, because the assertion narrows the code after it
`unknown`, because the generic `T` is erased by the assertion
questions.why: `asserts v is X` tells the compiler that if the call returns at all, the condition held, so control-flow analysis narrows `el` for the rest of the scope. A `v is X` type guard needs an `if` around the call; an assertion function acts like an inline `if (!el) throw`.
questions.asked: Assertion functions are the tidy way to fail fast on invariants, and they pair naturally with validation at a boundary.

choices: An error: `greet` expected 2 arguments, but got 1
Nothing; `this` is typed as `any` at a plain call site
Nothing; `'Hi'` binds to `this` and `greeting` is undefined
An error: a `this` of type `void` does not match `{ name: string }`
questions.why: A `this` parameter is a fake first parameter: it is erased from the output and does not count as an argument, it only types what `this` must be at the call. A bare call has `this: void`, so tsc rejects it, while `user.greet('Hi')` on an object with a `name` compiles.
questions.asked: It comes up when typing DOM handlers and callback APIs that rely on `this`, and it separates careful readers from skimmers.

choices: Nothing; `import type` is only a hint and the class is still imported
An error: `User` cannot be used as a value after `import type`
Nothing at compile time, but `new User` throws a ReferenceError
An error: only interfaces and type aliases can use `import type`
questions.why: `import type` is always erased from the output, so the name exists only in type positions and `new User` is an error. Importing a class this way is allowed when you only use it in annotations, which rules out the last choice. `verbatimModuleSyntax` builds on this: every import not marked `type` is emitted as written.
questions.asked: Type-only imports stop types from dragging runtime modules, and their side effects or cycles, into a bundle.

questions.q: With `isolatedModules` on, why does tsc reject this re-export?
questions.code:
// models.ts: export interface User { name: string }
export { User } from './models';
choices: A per-file transpiler cannot tell `User` is a type, so it would emit a runtime export
Interfaces cannot be re-exported at all, so consumers must import from `models`
`isolatedModules` forbids every re-export, so each export must be declared locally
The re-export creates a circular import that single-file transpilers cannot resolve
questions.why: esbuild, SWC and Babel compile one file at a time without type information, so they cannot know `User` has no runtime value and would emit an export that fails at load time. `export type { User }` states the intent, and plain value re-exports stay legal. `verbatimModuleSyntax` extends the same rule to imports.
questions.asked: Vite and Next.js templates turn this flag on, so the error is one you meet on day one.

questions.q: With `module: nodenext`, `"type": "module"` in package.json and other settings at their defaults, how must this import be written?
questions.code:
// math.ts exists alongside this file and exports add
import { add } from './math';
choices: As it is; tsc resolves `./math` to `math.ts` the way a bundler would
As `'./math.ts'`, naming the source file that actually exists on disk
As `'./math.js'`, naming the file that Node will load at runtime
As `'./math/index.js'`, since Node's ESM loader tries folders first
questions.why: Under `nodenext`, tsc models Node's ESM loader, which never guesses extensions, and imports name the emitted file, so you write `.js` even though only `math.ts` exists. `moduleResolution: bundler` drops the rule because Vite and webpack resolve extensionless relative paths. A `.ts` path needs `allowImportingTsExtensions` or `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`.
questions.asked: Choosing between `bundler` and `nodenext` is the first tsconfig decision on a new project, and it depends on what runs the output.

questions.q: This declaration file, which has no imports or exports, is included, yet `window.appVersion` is still a type error. What fixes it?
choices: Rename it to `window.ts`, since `.d.ts` files cannot contain `declare global`
Replace the `interface` with a `type`, since `Window` is a built-in type
List the file in the `types` array of tsconfig.json so it loads globally
Add `export {}`, so the file becomes a module and `declare global` is allowed
questions.why: `declare global` augments the global scope from inside a module; a file with no imports or exports is a script, so tsc rejects the block (silently, if skipLibCheck is on) and nothing is added. Add `export {}`, or drop the wrapper and declare `interface Window` at top level. Interface merging is what makes it work, so a `type` would clash instead.
questions.asked: Adding a global, or a field to a library's `Request` type, is routine and exposes whether you understand script versus module files.

choices: Both, since `onlyStrings` has a `handle` function in each case
Only `a`, since method parameters stay bivariant even under strict
Only `b`, since property functions are compared more loosely
Neither, since `strictFunctionTypes` rejects both of them
questions.why: `strictFunctionTypes` checks parameters contravariantly only for function-typed properties; members written with method syntax stay bivariant for compatibility with the DOM and older libraries. So `a` compiles and will call `trim` on a number at runtime, while `b` errors.
questions.asked: Few candidates know this hole exists, and it explains why some codebases declare callbacks as properties.

choices: Only `b`; excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals
Only `a`; literals are checked by shape, but variables must match exactly
Both; extra properties are always fine because typing is structural
Neither; `z` is not a property of `Point` in either declaration
questions.why: Structural typing lets an object with extra properties satisfy Point, so `b` is fine. As a typo guard, tsc additionally rejects unknown properties when an object literal is written directly against a type; once it passes through a variable that check no longer applies.
questions.asked: It explains why a misspelt optional option sometimes goes unnoticed, and it is a good probe of structural typing.

choices: `a`, because `{}` means an empty object literal
`c`, because `unknown` values must be narrowed first
`b`, because `object` means any non-primitive value
`a` and `b`, because a string is not an object type
questions.why: `{}` means any value except null and undefined, so a string fits; `object` excludes primitives; `unknown` accepts everything, and narrowing is only needed to use one, not to assign to it. For a plain object with unknown keys, `Record<string, unknown>` says what you mean.
questions.asked: Linters flag `{}` as a type for exactly this reason, and knowing why is a quick signal of type-system fluency.

choices: Both, because neither type declares a `string` index signature
`b`, because a type alias needs an explicit index signature
Neither, because every value is assignable to `unknown` anyway
`a`, because interfaces get no implicit index signature
questions.why: Object type aliases get an implicit index signature, so `t` fits `Record<string, unknown>`. Interfaces do not, because declaration merging could add incompatible members later. Spread the value (`{ ...i }`) or accept `object` in the helper's signature.
questions.asked: It surfaces when passing a typed DTO to a generic logging or serialising helper, and the error baffles people the first time.

questions.code:
type Box<T, U = T[]> = { item: T; list: U };
type B = Box<string>;
choices: `{ item: string; list: string[] }`, as a default may use T
`{ item: string; list: unknown }`, as defaults cannot read T
An error, as a default cannot refer to an earlier parameter
`{ item: string; list: T[] }`, left unresolved until used
questions.why: A type parameter default can reference any parameter declared before it, so omitting U makes it `T[]` with T already set to `string`. Defaults are resolved at instantiation, never left as a free `T`; only references to later parameters are rejected.
questions.asked: Defaults that build on earlier parameters are common in library types, and reading them is part of reading any `.d.ts`.

questions.q: What does tsc report for the last line?
choices: Nothing; K is `'id'` and V is inferred as `number`
An error: expected 2 type arguments, but got 1
Nothing; V falls back to `unknown` since it was skipped
An error: `42` is not assignable to type `string`
questions.why: TypeScript has no partial type-argument inference: once you pass any explicit type arguments, every parameter without a default must be supplied. Giving V a default would make the call legal, but V would then be the default, not inferred from `42`.
questions.asked: It explains why libraries split one generic call into curried steps such as `builder<Model>()(config)`.

choices: `a`, because a generic function type needs an explicit type argument
Neither, because T is inferred from the arrow function in each case
`b`, because the generic type `IdB` must be given its type argument
`a` and `b`, because an arrow function cannot take a generic type
questions.why: `IdA` is a non-generic type whose value is a generic function, so the caller picks T on every call. `IdB` is a generic type alias; using it without `<T>` is error 2314, because type aliases never infer their arguments from an initialiser.
questions.asked: Where the type parameter sits decides whether a callback works for any type or is fixed to one, which matters when typing handler props.

choices: `number | undefined`, taken from the first element in the array
An error: `'a'` is not assignable to type `number`
`unknown`, because the elements share no common type
`string | number | undefined`, from the array element union
questions.why: The argument `[1, 'a']` is typed `(string | number)[]` before inference, so there is one candidate and T becomes `string | number`. The 'not assignable' error only appears when T has two separate inference sites whose candidates conflict, such as `pair(1, 'one')`.
questions.asked: Predicting what T becomes from an argument is the core skill behind reading any generic signature.

choices: The `b` line, since `'email'` is not in `keyof` the user type
The `a` line, since `K` must be passed explicitly as `'age'`
Neither; `b` compiles and its value is typed as `unknown`
The `return`, since `obj[key]` needs a cast to `T[K]` first
questions.why: `K extends keyof T` limits keys to `'name' | 'age'` once T is inferred from `user`, so `'email'` is rejected at the call and `a` is typed `number`. The body needs no cast: indexing a T by a `K extends keyof T` yields exactly `T[K]`.
questions.asked: The `K extends keyof T` pattern is behind every typed `pick`, `sortBy` or form `setValue` helper.

questions.q: Why does this fail to compile?
choices: `find` cannot be called on a generic array without a type argument
Nothing tells tsc that T has an `id`, so the access is rejected
`id` is a number but `item.id` is inferred as a string property
Arrow callbacks inside generic functions lose their parameter types
questions.why: Inside the body an unconstrained T could be anything, even `number`, so only members every type has are allowed. Adding `T extends { id: number }` fixes it; the callback's `item` is correctly typed T, the problem is what T is known to contain.
questions.asked: Adding the right constraint instead of reaching for `any` is the first generic fix a reviewer looks for.

choices: `??` is not allowed on an optional generic parameter under strict
The literal `3` widens to `number`, but T needs the literal type
A caller may pick a T with more properties than `{ retries: 3 }`
Returning an object literal from a generic function needs `as const`
questions.why: T is chosen by the caller and can be any subtype of the constraint, such as `{ retries: number; url: string }`; the literal satisfies the constraint but not every possible T. tsc says it 'is assignable to the constraint of type T, but T could be instantiated with a different subtype'.
questions.asked: This error message confuses many developers, and explaining it shows you understand who chooses a type parameter.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.9, what is the type of `r`?
choices: `readonly ['a', 'b']`, as the `const` modifier always implies
`['a', 'b']`, a mutable tuple matching the mutable constraint
An error, because a readonly tuple is not assignable to `string[]`
`string[]`, because the readonly inference fails the constraint
questions.why: Since TypeScript 5.3, a `const` type parameter whose constraint is a mutable array infers a mutable literal tuple instead of falling back to `string[]` as 5.0 to 5.2 did. With a `readonly string[]` constraint the same call gives `readonly ['a', 'b']`; `const` only implies readonly where the constraint allows it.
questions.asked: Knowing how `const` type parameters interact with their constraint saves an `as const` at every call site.

questions.q: What does tsc report on the last line?
choices: An error: expected 2 arguments, as `A` is `[id: string, draft: boolean]`
Nothing, because rest parameters typed as `unknown[]` take any arguments
Nothing, because `A` is widened to `(string | boolean)[]` on inference
An error: `'42'` is not assignable to a parameter of type `unknown`
questions.why: A type parameter constrained to an array and used as `...args: A` is inferred as the callback's parameter tuple, labels included, so the wrapper keeps the exact signature. It does not widen to an array of the union; `unknown[]` is only the upper bound.
questions.asked: Typing wrappers like debounce, memoize or retry without losing the wrapped signature is an everyday higher-order-function task.

choices: `[x: number]`, from the first overload that was declared
`[x: Date]`, from the last overload that was declared
`[x: number] | [x: Date]`, one tuple for each overload
`[x: number | Date]`, from the implementation signature
questions.why: Inferring from an overloaded function type, as `Parameters` and `ReturnType` do with `infer`, uses the last signature only. The implementation signature is not part of the visible type at all, and there is no automatic union of overloads.
questions.asked: It bites anyone wrapping an overloaded API such as `addEventListener` with a generic helper.

choices: `T`, the free type parameter carried out of the function
`any`, because the type parameter was never instantiated
`unknown`, because T is replaced by its constraint first
`never`, because there is no call site to infer T from
questions.why: When a generic signature is matched against a non-generic pattern, its type parameters are replaced by their constraints, and an unconstrained T has constraint `unknown`. It is not `any`; for a specific result use an instantiation expression, `ReturnType<typeof identity<string>>`.
questions.asked: Deriving types from generic functions comes up when typing factories and hooks, and the `unknown` result surprises people.

choices: A `Map<string, User>`, because type arguments invoke the function
A syntax error, since type arguments require call parentheses
A wrapper that tsc emits to pre-bind K and V for later calls
A function typed `() => Map<string, User>`, with nothing called
questions.why: An instantiation expression applies type arguments without calling, so `makeUserMap` has type `() => Map<string, User>`. It emits as a plain reference to `makeMap`: no wrapper is generated and nothing runs.
questions.asked: Instantiation expressions are how you name a specialised version of a generic function or class without wrapping it.

choices: `static shared`, since statics cannot use the class type parameter
`items`, since a generic field needs a definite assignment `!`
`add`, since methods on a generic class must repeat the `<T>`
The class header, since a generic class needs `T extends object`
questions.why: There is one static per class, shared by `Store<string>` and `Store<number>` alike, so its type cannot depend on T (error 2302). Instance members may use T freely, and methods do not redeclare it.
questions.asked: It tests whether you think of a generic class as one runtime object with many type views.

questions.q: In a `.tsx` file, why is this written `<T,>` rather than `<T>`?
questions.code: const first = <T,>(xs: T[]) => xs[0];
choices: The comma marks T as optional so callers may leave it out
Without it, `<T>` is parsed as the opening of a JSX element
Arrow functions need a trailing comma in every type list
It makes T default to `unknown` instead of `any` in TSX
questions.why: In `.tsx`, `<T>(...)` is ambiguous with a JSX tag, so the parser needs a hint that it is a type parameter list: a trailing comma or a constraint such as `<T extends unknown>`. In `.ts` files `<T>` alone is fine, and the comma changes nothing about defaults.
questions.asked: Anyone writing generic React helpers hits this parser quirk in their first week.

choices: `unknown[]`, since U appears only in the callback return type
`string[]`, since U is taken from the first argument as well
`number[]`, since U is inferred from what the callback returns
An error, since `s` is implicitly `any` inside the callback
questions.why: T is fixed from the array first, which contextually types `s` as `string`, and then U is inferred from what the callback returns. That left-to-right flow is why data arguments usually come before callbacks in generic APIs; `s` is never implicitly `any` here.
questions.asked: Knowing that inference flows from earlier arguments into callbacks explains many API designs and many confusing errors.

questions.code:
type ToNum<S> = S extends `${infer X extends number}` ? X : never;
type N = ToNum<'42'>;
choices: `number`, since `infer` in a template gives only the wide type
`'42'`, since infer keeps the matched text as a string literal
`never`, since the string `'42'` is not assignable to number
`42`, the number literal parsed from the matched string text
questions.why: `infer X extends number` inside a template literal type asks tsc to parse the matched text as a numeric literal, so `'42'` yields `42`. Without the `extends number` clause X would be `'42'`; if the text were not numeric the match would fail and give `never`.
questions.asked: Typed route params and parsers use it to turn `/items/:id` style strings into real numeric types.

questions.code:
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T;
type A = Unwrap<Promise<Promise<number>>>;
choices: `Promise<number>`, since Unwrap strips one layer only
`number`, since `infer` keeps unwrapping nested promises
`Promise<Promise<number>>`, as nested ones never match
`unknown`, since U cannot be inferred through two layers
questions.why: The conditional matches once and returns the inner type, which is still a promise. The built-in `Awaited<T>` is recursive, calling itself on the inner value, which is why it gives `number` here and is what `async` return types use.
questions.asked: Writing an unwrap helper and then realising why `Awaited` is recursive is a common first `infer` exercise.

questions.code:
type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer X)[] ? X : T;
type E = ElementOf<string[] | number>;
choices: `string[] | number`, as the union as a whole is not an array
`string | number`, as each union member is checked separately
`string`, as members that fail the test are dropped from it
`never`, as `number` fails the array test for the whole union
questions.why: A conditional on a naked type parameter distributes over a union: `string[]` gives `string`, and `number` takes the false branch and stays `number`. Only a wrapped check such as `[T] extends [...]` tests the union as a whole, which would give back `string[] | number`.
questions.asked: Distribution explains most surprising conditional-type results in code review.

questions.code:
type Label<T> = T extends true ? 'on' : 'off';
type R = Label<boolean>;
choices: `'off'`, since `boolean` as a whole is not assignable to true
`'on'`, since `boolean` is checked against its first member
`'on' | 'off'`, since `boolean` is the union `true | false`
`string`, since both branches widen to their common type
questions.why: `boolean` is literally `true | false`, so a distributive conditional runs once per member and unions the results. People expect a single answer for `boolean`; wrapping as `[T] extends [true]` tests it whole and gives `'off'`.
questions.asked: Flag-driven types such as `Options<Strict extends boolean>` break in exactly this way.

questions.code:
type IsStr<T> = T extends string ? 'yes' : 'no';
type R = IsStr<any>;
choices: `'yes'`, since `any` is assignable to every type
`'no'`, since `any` is not a subtype of string
`any`, since conditional types propagate `any`
`'yes' | 'no'`, since `any` takes both branches
questions.why: When the checked type is `any`, tsc cannot pick a branch and returns the union of both. That is why naive type-equality helpers built from two `extends` checks misreport `any`, and why type-testing libraries use a stricter comparison.
questions.asked: It shows you know the special cases (`any`, `never`) that make hand-rolled type utilities unreliable.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.9, why is the `return` rejected?
choices: The conditional on an unresolved T is deferred, so neither value fits it
The ternary widens `1` and `'one'` to `number | string`, which is too wide
Narrowing `kind` narrows T, but `'one'` still fails for the `'str'` branch
Conditional return types are only allowed on overload signatures
questions.why: Inside the body T is still generic, so `T extends 'num' ? number : string` stays deferred and neither `1` nor `'one'` is assignable to it; narrowing `kind` does not narrow T. The usual fixes are overloads or one contained cast behind the well-typed signature.
questions.asked: Conditional return types look elegant, and knowing their implementation cost stops people over-using them.

questions.q: Why does this compile, although `createdAt` is clearly not a date?
choices: Optional properties accept `{}` because excess checks are skipped
Date is an object, so it maps to a type with every method optional
DeepPartial stops at one level, so `createdAt` becomes `unknown`
`{}` is the empty object type, which every type is assignable to
questions.why: The recursion treats `Date` like any object and maps its methods into optional properties, which `{}` satisfies. Real DeepPartial helpers stop at built-ins with a check such as `T[K] extends Date | Function ? T[K] : DeepPartial<T[K]>`; a plain `Partial<Post>` would reject `{}` for a Date.
questions.asked: Recursive utility types in real code need base cases for built-ins, and a reviewer should spot the missing one.

choices: `'id' | 'author'`, since the recursion adds nested keys as types only
`'id' | 'name' | 'author'`, with nested keys flattened to one level
`'id' | 'author' | 'author.name'`, each nested key under its parent
`'id' | 'author.name'`, since object-valued keys become only paths
questions.why: For each key the mapped type yields the key itself and, for object values, the key joined to the paths of the nested type; indexing with `[keyof T & string]` unions them. Form libraries type `register('author.name')` this way; `& string` drops number and symbol keys that cannot go in a template.
questions.asked: Dot-path types power form and i18n libraries, and reading one shows real fluency with recursion.

questions.code:
type Last<T extends unknown[]> = T extends [...unknown[], infer X] ? X : never;
type L = Last<[string, number, boolean]>;
choices: `string`, since `infer` binds to the first unmatched element
`never`, since a rest element must come last in the pattern
`string | number | boolean`, as the rest absorbs everything
`boolean`, since the rest element takes all but the final one
questions.why: Variadic tuple types allow a rest element in any position, so `[...unknown[], infer X]` matches any non-empty tuple and binds its final element. The rule that rest must be last applies to parameter lists, not tuple types; an empty tuple would give `never`.
questions.asked: Tuple patterns are how middleware chains and pipe helpers type their first and last functions.

questions.code:
type Both<T> = T extends { a: infer X; b: infer X } ? X : never;
type V = Both<{ a: string; b: number }>;
choices: `string | number`, a union of the candidates found for X
`string`, the first candidate, with `b` failing to match
`never`, since X cannot be string and number at once
`string & number`, the intersection of both candidates
questions.why: Several `infer X` sites in covariant positions, such as properties, produce a union of the candidates. In contravariant positions, such as two function parameters, the candidates are intersected instead, which is the trick behind `UnionToIntersection`.
questions.asked: It separates people who can read advanced library types from those who copy them.

choices: `{ save: 'save'; load: 'load' }`, the object before indexing
`'save' | 'load'`, with the `never` for `id` dropped from it
`'id' | 'save' | 'load'`, since every key maps to something
`'save' | 'load' | never`, which cannot be simplified further
questions.why: The mapped type turns each property into its own key or `never`, and indexing it with `[keyof T]` collects the values as a union, where `never` vanishes. It is the classic way to pick keys by value type; since TS 4.1, key remapping with `as` can filter keys directly.
questions.asked: Selecting keys by value type is needed for typed form fields, sort keys and event maps.

questions.code:
type StringProps<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K] };
type S = StringProps<{ id: number; name: string; nick?: string }>;
choices: `{ name: string; nick?: string }`, keeping the optional modifier
`{ name: string; nick: string }`, since `as` drops the modifiers
`{ name: string }`, since `nick` reads as `string | undefined` here
`{ id: never; name: string; nick?: string }`, with no key removed
questions.why: Reading an optional property through `T[K]` includes `undefined`, and `string | undefined` does not extend `string`, so `nick` is filtered out. Test `NonNullable<T[K]>` to keep optional string fields; when a key does survive, `as` remapping keeps its modifiers.
questions.asked: Filtering keys by value type is common, and silently losing optional fields is the bug that ships.

questions.code:
type Stringify<T> = { [K in keyof T]: string };
type R = Stringify<[number, boolean]>;
choices: An object with keys `0`, `1`, `length` and every array method
`string[]`, since mapping over a tuple loses its fixed length
`{ 0: string; 1: string }`, a plain object with numeric keys
`[string, string]`, since the mapping applies to each element
questions.why: A homomorphic mapped type (`[K in keyof T]` with T a type parameter) instantiated with a tuple maps only the element positions and keeps the tuple shape, which is why `Partial<[a, b]>` is `[a?, b?]`. Only a mapping over a concrete array type, not a parameter, would touch `length` and the methods.
questions.asked: Typing `Promise.all`-style helpers relies on mapped types preserving tuples.

questions.code:
type Without<T, X> = { [K in keyof T as Exclude<K, X>]: T[K] };
type Public = Without<{ readonly id: number; nick?: string; pw: string }, 'pw'>;
choices: `{ readonly id: number; nick?: string }`, modifiers kept
`{ id: number; nick: string | undefined }`, modifiers lost
`{ readonly id: number; nick?: string; pw: never }`
`{ id: number; nick?: string }`, readonly stripped by `as`
questions.why: Key remapping with `as` still iterates `keyof T`, so the mapped type stays homomorphic and copies `readonly` and `?` from the source. Keys remapped to `never` are removed outright rather than kept as `never`-typed properties.
questions.asked: Building DTO types by removing sensitive keys needs you to know whether readonly and optional survive.

questions.code:
type Req<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type R = Req<{ note?: string }>;
choices: `{ note: string | undefined }`, required but still nullable
`{ note: string }`, with the `undefined` from `?` removed too
`{ note?: string }`, since `-?` applies only to readonly keys
`{ note: never }`, since an optional value cannot be required
questions.why: `-?` removes the optional modifier and the `undefined` that `?` added, which is exactly how the built-in `Required<T>` works. Mapping without `-?` would keep `note?: string`, since homomorphic mapped types copy modifiers from the source.
questions.asked: Knowing how `Required` is built helps you write variants such as "required except id".

choices: `'id' | 'last4' | 'iban'`, every key of either member
`never`, since the two types have different shapes
`'id'`, the only key both members are known to have
`string`, since keys of a union widen to `string`
questions.why: A value of `Card | Bank` is only guaranteed to have the keys common to both, so `keyof` of a union is the intersection of the members' keys. `keyof (Card & Bank)` gives all three; for per-member keys, distribute with `T extends unknown ? keyof T : never`.
questions.asked: It explains why generic helpers over union types suddenly accept only the shared fields.

questions.code: type Ev = `${'user' | 'order'}:${'created' | 'deleted'}`;
choices: Two, pairing the unions position by position
Four, but only once `Ev` is used as a key type
One, since template literal types never expand unions
Four: every combination of the two unions
questions.why: Unions inside a template literal type expand as a cross product, so two members times two gives four string literals such as `'user:created'`. It is handy for event names, but it multiplies quickly and tsc refuses results beyond 100,000 members.
questions.asked: Typed event buses and permission strings are usually built this way.

choices: `d`, since `Number('1_000')` does not parse as a number
`c`, since exponent notation is not a numeric literal form
`b`, since `${number}` accepts only non-negative numbers
`a`, since `${number}` in a template means integers only
questions.why: A string matches `${number}` when JavaScript can convert that text to a number, so decimals, signs and exponents all pass. Numeric separators such as `1_000` are only source-code syntax: `Number('1_000')` is `NaN`, so `d` is rejected.
questions.asked: CSS-unit and version-string types use `${number}`, and knowing what it accepts avoids false confidence.

choices: `string`, since `infer` inside a template always widens
`'id' | 'postId'`, one member for each `:param` segment
`'id'`, since the recursion stops after the first match
`'id/posts/:postId'`, since `infer` matches greedily
questions.why: Each `infer` followed by a literal delimiter captures the shortest text up to that delimiter, so the first match takes `id` and recurses on the rest, where the second branch captures `postId`. Typed routers turn a path string into a params type this way.
questions.asked: Typed route params are the most common real use of recursive template literal types.

questions.code: type Changed<T> = `${keyof T & string}Changed`;
choices: Without it, the keys are widened to plain `string` first
`keyof` returns an array of keys that must be flattened
`keyof T` may include symbol keys, which a template rejects
It forces the property names to lowercase for event names
questions.why: `keyof T` is `string | number | symbol` for an arbitrary T, and a symbol cannot be interpolated into a template literal type, so tsc rejects `${keyof T}`. Intersecting with `string` keeps only the string keys; the literal key names are not widened either way.
questions.asked: Anyone generating event or getter names from a model type writes this intersection.

questions.code:
type User = { id: number; name: string; active: boolean };
type V = User['id' | 'name'];
choices: `{ id: number; name: string }`, like a `Pick` of both keys
`[number, string]`, a tuple in the order of the keys
An error, since an index type must be a single key
`number | string`, a union of the two property types
questions.why: Indexed access with a union of keys returns the union of the property types; it does not build an object. `Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>` is the one that keeps the object shape.
questions.asked: Indexed access types are how you reuse a field type without copying it.

questions.code:
function connect(url: string, opts: { retries: number }) {}
type Opts = Parameters<typeof connect>[1];
choices: `{ retries: number }`, the second parameter's type
`string`, since tuple indexes in types start at 1
`[opts: { retries: number }]`, a one-element tuple
An error, since `typeof` cannot be used on functions
questions.why: `typeof connect` lifts the function's type into type space, `Parameters` turns its parameter list into a tuple, and `[1]` indexes the second element. It is the standard way to reuse an options type that a library never exported.
questions.asked: Pulling unexported types out of third-party functions is a daily need.

questions.code:
type User = { name: string; address?: { city: string } };
type Addr = User['address'];
choices: `{ city: string }`, since indexing strips the optional marker
`{ city: string } | undefined`, as the property is optional
`{ city?: string }`, since optionality moves to the members
An error, since optional properties cannot be indexed
questions.why: Indexed access returns the property's read type, which for an optional property includes `undefined`. Wrap it as `NonNullable<User['address']>` when you want the object type alone, for example to type a sub-component's props.
questions.asked: Deriving child prop types from a parent model trips on this `undefined` constantly.

questions.code:
enum Color { Red = 'red', Green = 'green' }
type Name = keyof typeof Color;
choices: `'red' | 'green'`, the enum's string values
`Color`, the union of the enum's members
`'Red' | 'Green'`, the enum's member names
`string`, since enum keys are not literal types
questions.why: `typeof Color` is the type of the runtime enum object, whose keys are the member names, so `keyof` gives `'Red' | 'Green'`. The values `'red' | 'green'` would come from `${Color}` in a template literal type, and `Color` itself is the union of the members.
questions.asked: Mapping between enum names and values is common when parsing query strings or config.

questions.q: In a type position, how do `User` and `typeof User` differ?
choices: They do not; for classes `typeof` aliases the instance type
`User` is the constructor type; `typeof User` is an instance
`typeof User` is `'function'`, the string `typeof` returns
`User` is the instance type; `typeof User` is the class itself
questions.why: A class declares two things: an instance type named `User`, and a constructor value whose type, `typeof User`, includes `new (name: string) => User` and statics such as `create`. Type-position `typeof` never produces the runtime string `'function'`.
questions.asked: Passing classes to factories and DI containers needs the constructor type, not the instance type.

questions.q: Why is the last call rejected?
choices: Callers see only the overloads, and none takes three arguments
Optional parameters are not allowed in an overload implementation
Overloads need the implementation to declare its return type
Arguments are checked against the first overload signature only
questions.why: The implementation signature is invisible to callers; only the overload signatures are, and neither accepts three arguments. The implementation may use defaults, optional parameters and an inferred return type as long as it is compatible with every overload; add a third overload to expose `loud`.
questions.asked: It checks that you know overloads replace, rather than add to, the implementation signature.

choices: `number`, since tsc picks the most specific overload
`string`, since the first matching overload wins
`string | number`, since both overloads match `'a'`
An error, since the overloads overlap ambiguously
questions.why: Overload resolution tries signatures in declaration order and stops at the first that accepts the arguments, so the broad `unknown` overload hides the specific one. Order overloads from most specific to most general; tsc does not rank them by specificity.
questions.asked: Misordered overloads are a quiet bug in hand-written `.d.ts` files.

choices: No: `where` returns `Query`, which has no `active` method
No: a method cannot return the polymorphic `this` type
Yes: a `this` return type means the receiver's own class
Yes, because subclass methods are merged into the base
questions.why: The polymorphic `this` type resolves to the type of the object the method is called on, so `where` on a `UserQuery` returns `UserQuery`. Annotating `where(): Query` would lose the subclass methods, which is the bug fluent builders usually hit.
questions.asked: Query builders and fluent APIs rely on `this` types to chain subclass methods.

choices: `x`, since `b` is excess for the `{ a: number }` member
Neither, since every property exists in some union member
`x` and `y`, since excess checks run on each member alone
`y`, since the discriminant picks one member to check against
questions.why: For an untagged union, a fresh literal only needs each property to exist in some member, so `x` passes. When the union has a discriminant, tsc first narrows to the member matching `kind: 'a'` and then reports `b` as excess.
questions.asked: Excess property checks on unions are subtle, and knowing when they are lax explains bugs in option objects.

choices: `string`, taken from the `Record<string, Route>` it satisfies
`'home' | 'about'`, since `satisfies` keeps the inferred type
`never`, since `satisfies` erases the object's own key names
`string | number`, the key type of any record with string keys
questions.why: `satisfies` checks the value against the type but leaves the variable with its own inferred type, so the literal keys survive. Annotating `const routes: Record<string, Route>` would make `Name` plain `string` and let typos such as `routes.abuot` compile.
questions.asked: Config maps that are both checked and precisely keyed are the main reason `satisfies` exists.

questions.q: In TypeScript 5.5+, why is `names` still `(string | undefined)[]`?
questions.code:
const raw = ['ann', undefined, 'bo'];
const names = raw.filter((x) => !!x);
choices: Predicates are only inferred from `!==` checks, never from `!!`
A false result may be the empty string, so it is not `x is string`
Predicates are only inferred for arrows with a block body
`filter` uses inferred predicates only on `as const` arrays
questions.why: An inferred predicate `x is string` must also mean a false result proves `x` is not a string, and `''` is a string that returns false. tsc therefore infers nothing; write `x !== undefined` or an explicit predicate. Truthiness of an `object | undefined` would infer fine.
questions.asked: It shows you understand what a type predicate claims in both branches.

questions.q: What is the type of `port` on the last line?
choices: `number | undefined`, since assertions narrow only a named argument
`boolean`, since the asserted value was the comparison result
`number`, since `asserts cond` narrows as if the condition held
`unknown`, since the parameter `cond` is typed as `unknown`
questions.why: `asserts cond` tells tsc that if the call returns, the argument expression was truthy, so whatever it implies, here `port !== undefined`, holds for the rest of the scope. This is how Node's `assert` is typed, and it works on any condition, not only a bare variable.
questions.asked: Invariant helpers built on `asserts cond` replace many non-null assertions in real code.

questions.q: What is the type of `user[key]` inside the `if`?
choices: An error, since `key` is still `string` and cannot index `user`
`unknown`, because the predicate only narrows to `PropertyKey`
`number`, the type of the first property the key could name
`string | number`, since `key` narrowed to `'id' | 'name'`
questions.why: A type predicate can narrow any parameter, and `k is keyof T` narrows `key` to `'id' | 'name'`, so the access is the union of both property types. tsc never checks that `k in o` proves the claim, and it is in fact unsound for inherited keys such as `'toString'`.
questions.asked: Safe dynamic key access is a frequent code-review topic, and so is the trust a predicate asks for.

questions.q: What does the `out` annotation on T do?
choices: Declares T covariant, which tsc checks against how T is used
Makes T readonly, so implementations cannot mutate the value
Allows T to be inferred from return types at call sites only
Turns off variance checks for T, as method bivariance does
questions.why: The `in` and `out` modifiers (TS 4.7+) state a type parameter's variance so tsc can compare `Producer<Dog>` with `Producer<Animal>` without measuring it structurally, and tsc errors if the annotation contradicts the members. They help checker performance and documentation; they never switch checking off or change inference.
questions.asked: Variance annotations appear in library typings and are a quick test of whether you understand co- and contravariance.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this declaration?
choices: Nothing, since method parameters are bivariant and so fit `out`
An error: T is used in an input position but is marked `out`
Nothing, since variance annotations are documentation only
An error: `out` is allowed on type aliases, not on interfaces
questions.why: tsc verifies the annotation by checking that `Sink<Sub>` is assignable to `Sink<Super>`, and method-shorthand parameters are compared bivariantly, so the check passes. Declared as a property, `write: (value: T) => void`, the parameter is contravariant and the same `out` is error 2636: the annotations are checked, not decorative.
questions.asked: It shows you can tell producers from consumers, which is what variance comes down to.

choices: Only `new Repo()`, since an abstract class cannot be constructed
Only `UserRepo`, since it leaves the abstract `find` unimplemented
The `UserRepo` declaration and the `new Repo()` call
Neither, since abstract members default to throwing at runtime
questions.why: A concrete subclass must implement every abstract member, so `UserRepo` is error 2515, and an abstract class can never be constructed directly (error 2511). Abstract members have no runtime body at all; they exist only as a type-level contract.
questions.asked: Abstract base classes for repositories and services are common in NestJS-style back ends.

questions.q: What does tsc report for this code?
choices: An error on `push`, since tuples have a fixed length
An error on `.length`, which is typed as the literal `2`
Nothing, since `[number, number]` is an alias of `number[]`
Nothing; `push` is inherited from `Array` and unrestricted
questions.why: Tuple types extend `Array`, so mutating methods such as `push` stay available, while `pair.length` is still typed `2` although it is 3 at runtime. Declare it `readonly [number, number]` to remove the mutating methods.
questions.asked: It is a small, concrete example of where the type system is deliberately unsound.

choices: `typeof Mailer` and `[string, number]`
`Mailer` and `[host: string, port: number]`
`Mailer` and `{ host: string; port: number }`
`object` and `(string | number)[]`
questions.why: Both utilities work on the constructor type `typeof Mailer`: `InstanceType` gives what `new` returns (the instance type `Mailer`), and `ConstructorParameters` gives the argument list as a labelled tuple. They are the class equivalents of `ReturnType` and `Parameters`.
questions.asked: DI containers and factories pass classes around as values, and these utilities type them.

questions.code: type Verb = Uppercase<'get' | 'post'>;
choices: An error, since it needs a single literal
`string`, since intrinsic types widen
`'Get' | 'Post'`, in title case
`'GET' | 'POST'`
questions.why: `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize` and `Uncapitalize` are compiler intrinsics that map over each member of a union of string literals. `Capitalize` is the one that only changes the first letter.
questions.asked: These show up in typed HTTP clients and event-name helpers, so reading them is expected.

questions.code: type R = Readonly<string[]>;
choices: `readonly [string]`, a single-element tuple
`string[]`, since `Readonly` only affects objects
`{ readonly [n: number]: string }` without methods
`readonly string[]`
questions.why: Homomorphic mapped types like `Readonly` treat arrays specially and produce `readonly string[]` (a `ReadonlyArray<string>`), which drops `push`, `splice` and other mutators while keeping `map` and `filter`.
questions.asked: Readonly arrays in function signatures are a common review suggestion, so knowing the equivalent spellings helps.

questions.code: type Flags = { [K in 'dark' | 'beta']: boolean };
choices: `{ dark: boolean; beta: boolean }`
`{ [key: string]: boolean }`
`{ dark?: boolean; beta?: boolean }`
`Record<string, 'dark' | 'beta'>`
questions.why: A mapped type iterates over any union of keys, not only `keyof` something; each member becomes a required property. This is exactly how `Record<K, V>` is defined.
questions.asked: Understanding that `Record` is just a mapped type is the first step to reading utility types.

choices: `string | number`, the key types JSON allows
`string`, since keys are always strings
`string | number | symbol`
`never`, since `any` has no known keys
questions.why: Property keys in JavaScript can be strings, numbers (converted to strings) or symbols, so the most general key type is that union, also available as `PropertyKey`. Utilities like `Omit` constrain their keys with `K extends keyof any`.
questions.asked: It explains constraints you see in library typings and why `Omit` accepts any key.

choices: `number | string` and `number`
`number | string` and `2`
`number` and `2`
`[number, string]` and `number`
questions.why: Indexing a tuple with `number` gives the union of its element types, and its `length` is the literal `2` because the length is fixed. For a plain array, `length` would be `number`.
questions.asked: Indexed access on tuples and arrays is how element types are pulled out of `as const` lists.

choices: `{ type: 'add' }`, the shape passed as the filter
`Action`, as `Extract` matches on shared keys
`never`, as neither member equals the filter
`{ type: 'add'; item: string }`
questions.why: `Extract<T, U>` keeps the members of `T` that are assignable to `U`, and a member only needs the `type` property to match, so it works as a lookup by discriminant. It does not require the member to be identical to `U`.
questions.asked: Pulling one variant out of an action or event union is common in reducers and handlers.

questions.q: What does `declare module '*.svg' { const src: string; export default src; }` do?
choices: Types every `.svg` import as a default `string`
Loads SVG files as strings at runtime
Makes tsc copy SVG files into `outDir`
Validates that each SVG file is well-formed
questions.why: A wildcard module declaration tells the compiler what importing a matching path returns. It is purely a type claim; the bundler is what actually turns the import into a URL, so the declaration must match the bundler's behaviour.
questions.asked: Asset imports in Vite or webpack projects need this, and the `/// <reference>` alternative is a common follow-up.

questions.q: What does `/// <reference types="vite/client" />` in `src/vite-env.d.ts` give a Vite project?
choices: Types for `import.meta.env` and asset imports like `.svg`
A runtime polyfill for `import.meta` in older browsers
Type-checking during `vite dev`, which is otherwise off
Access to Vite plugin APIs from application code
questions.why: The directive pulls Vite's ambient declarations into the program: `ImportMetaEnv`, `import.meta.hot` and wildcard modules for assets. It has no runtime effect and does not make Vite type-check.
questions.asked: Everyone has seen this file; knowing what it does shows you read your config rather than copy it.

choices: Line A, because the type argument has extra properties
Line B, because the type argument has no `id`
Line C, because `save` expects exactly `{ id: string }`
None, because constraints are checked at runtime
questions.why: The constraint lets the class body rely on `row.id`, and every type argument must satisfy it. Extra properties are fine, so line A is valid and `save` then expects the full `{ id; name }` type.
questions.asked: Generic repositories and caches are classic "write a generic" interview tasks.

choices: Code outside the class must use `Money.fromPounds`
It makes `Money` instances immutable after creation
It prevents `Money` from being used as a type
It hides `cents` from code outside the class
questions.why: `new Money(...)` is only allowed inside the class, so every instance goes through the factory, which can validate or normalise input. `readonly` is what stops reassignment of `cents`, and it stays publicly readable.
questions.asked: Value objects with validated factories are a common modelling pattern in both TS and C#.

choices: `(string | undefined)[]`, since `filter` keeps its input type
`T[]`, since `T` cannot be inferred here
`unknown[]`, since the guard is generic
`string[]`, since the guard narrows each element
questions.why: `filter` has an overload that accepts a type predicate and returns `S[]`; `T` is inferred as `string` from the array. This generic guard predates 5.5 inferred predicates and is still common in utility modules.
questions.asked: A reusable `isDefined` is one of the most common small generics in real codebases.

questions.code:
type User = { email?: string | null };
type E = NonNullable<User['email']>;
choices: `string`
`string | null`
`string | undefined`
`never`
questions.why: Indexing an optional property includes `undefined`, and `NonNullable` removes both `null` and `undefined`, leaving `string`. It is defined as `T & {}`.
questions.asked: Deriving the "present" type of an optional field is common when writing guards and form handlers.

questions.code:
type Status = 'open' | 'closed' | 'merged';
type Counts = Partial<Record<Status, number>>;
choices: `{ open: 1, pending: 2 }`
`{ open: 1 }`
questions.why: `Record<Status, number>` requires every status; wrapping it in `Partial` makes each key optional but still rejects unknown keys and wrong value types. It is the right type for counts where zero entries are omitted.
questions.asked: Aggregations keyed by a status union are common in dashboards and reports.

questions.code:
type User = { id: string; email: string; createdAt: Date };
type Draft = Omit<User, 'id' | 'createAt'>;
choices: An error: `'createAt'` is not a key of `User`
An error only when a `Draft` value is created
`Draft` is `{ email: string }`, as the typo is corrected
`Draft` is `{ email: string; createdAt: Date }`, no error
questions.why: `Omit` constrains its keys only to `keyof any`, so a misspelt key is silently ignored and `createdAt` stays in the type. `Pick` does check its keys; some teams add a strict `StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T>` for this reason.
questions.asked: It is a real source of wrong DTO types, and knowing the asymmetry with `Pick` shows careful reading of library types.

questions.code:
type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };
type N = Nullable<{ id: number; tags?: string[] }>;
choices: `{ id: number | null; tags: string[] | null }`
`{ id: number | null; tags?: string[] | null | undefined }`
`{ id: number; tags?: string[] } | null`
`{ id?: number | null; tags?: string[] | null }`
questions.why: Mapping over `keyof T` is homomorphic, so optional and readonly modifiers carry over; `tags` stays optional and gains `| null`. The whole object does not become nullable, only each property.
questions.asked: Writing a small mapped type like this is a common interview exercise.

questions.code:
type Json =
  | string | number | boolean | null
  | Json[]
  | { [key: string]: Json };
choices: No, because its methods are not `Json` values
Yes, because a `Date` is an object with string keys
Yes, because `JSON.stringify` can serialise dates
No, because recursive types reject all class instances
questions.why: To match the index signature, every property of `Date` must be `Json`, and its methods are functions, so it is rejected. That is the point: a `Json` type forces you to convert dates to strings before serialising.
questions.asked: A `Json` type for cache or queue payloads is common, and it shows you understand recursive types and index signatures.

choices: `{ email: string } | null`
`unknown`
`{ name: 'signup' }`
`{ email: string }`
questions.why: `Extract` selects the `signup` member, and indexed access reads its `payload`. Indexing the whole union (`Event['payload']`) would give the union of all payloads instead.
questions.asked: Typed event buses and analytics trackers are built on exactly this lookup.

questions.q: What properties can you read on a `NoId` value without narrowing?
choices: Only `kind`, typed `'circle' | 'square'`
`kind`, `radius` and `side`, as before
None, as `Omit` on a union yields `{}`
`kind` plus whichever member matches first
questions.why: `Omit` is not distributive: `keyof Shape` is only the shared keys, so the result is a single object `{ kind: 'circle' | 'square' }` and the variants are lost. A distributive version, `T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never`, keeps them.
questions.asked: Deriving "create" types from union entities hits this, and it is a favourite senior-review catch.

questions.q: Which fix makes `Omit` keep each member of a union?
choices: `type D<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>` with a stricter key
`type D<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends unknown ? Omit<T, K> : never`
`type D<T, K extends PropertyKey> = Omit<T & {}, K>`
`type D<T, K extends PropertyKey> = { [P in Exclude<keyof T, K>]: T[P] }`
questions.why: A conditional type on a naked type parameter distributes over unions, so `Omit` runs once per member and the results are re-joined. The other forms still compute `keyof` of the whole union, which is only the shared keys.
questions.asked: Writing `DistributiveOmit` is a classic intermediate type-level exercise with a real use in form and DTO types.

questions.q: Which declaration adds a typed `user` to Express 5 request objects?
choices: `interface Request { user?: User }` in any `.ts` file
`declare global { var user: User }` in the auth middleware
`type Request = express.Request & { user?: User }` exported globally
`declare module 'express-serve-static-core' { interface Request { user?: User } }`
questions.why: Express's `Request` interface lives in `express-serve-static-core`, and module augmentation merges your property into it, so every handler sees `req.user`. A local interface or alias is a different type; a global variable is not on the request at all.
questions.asked: Auth middleware that attaches a user is universal, and typing it properly is a common Node interview question.

choices: Line A, because a brand cannot be created by assertion
Line B, because a plain `string` lacks the brand
Line C, because branded strings lose string methods
None, because brands are erased before type-checking
questions.why: The brand is a phantom property that no plain string has, so only values passed through `asUserId` (ideally a validating constructor) are accepted. The type is still a `string`, so string methods work, and nothing exists at runtime.
questions.asked: Branded IDs prevent mixing `UserId` and `OrderId`, and interviewers want to see you can write and use one.

choices: Asserting at compile time that `parse` returns exactly `User`
Checking at runtime that `parse` returns a valid `User`
Generating a JSON schema for `User` from the function
Mocking `parse` so that it returns a `User` fixture
questions.why: Type assertions like `expectTypeOf` do nothing at runtime; they fail type-checking (`vitest --typecheck` or tsc) if the inferred type drifts. They are how libraries and shared utilities test their types, alongside `@ts-expect-error` for negative cases.
questions.asked: Testing types is part of maintaining shared utility types, and knowing the tools marks a senior-leaning candidate.

questions.code:
const users = [{ id: 'a', name: 'Ann' }];
const byId = Object.fromEntries(users.map((u) => [u.id, u]));
choices: `Record<'a', { id: string; name: string }>`
`{ [k: string]: { id: string; name: string } }`
`Map<string, { id: string; name: string }>`
`any`, since the tuples are not inferred
questions.why: `fromEntries` accepts an iterable of key-value pairs and returns a string-indexed object of the value type. The keys are not tracked as literals, and it builds a plain object, not a `Map`.
questions.asked: Indexing lists by ID is everyday CRUD code, and it helps to know what type you get back.

questions.q: With `lib` including `es2024`, what is the type of `groups`?
choices: `Record<'todo' | 'done', Task[]>`
`{ [k: string]: Task[] }`
`Map<'todo' | 'done', Task[]>`
`Partial<Record<'todo' | 'done', Task[]>>`
questions.why: A group only exists if at least one item produced its key, so the lib types make every key optional and `groups.todo` is `Task[] | undefined`. A hand-rolled `groupBy` returning `Record<K, T[]>` claims every key exists, which is unsound.
questions.asked: ES2024 `groupBy` replaces many Lodash calls, and its honest return type is a good discussion point.

questions.code:
const pair: [number, number] = [1, 2];
const doubled = pair.map((n) => n * 2);
choices: `number[]`, since `map` returns a plain array
`[number, number]`, since `map` keeps the length
`readonly number[]`, since tuples are readonly
`[number, ...number[]]`, since it is non-empty
questions.why: `map` is declared on `Array<T>` as returning `U[]`, so tuple-ness is lost even though the length is preserved at runtime. Annotate the result or use a mapped type over the tuple when the fixed length matters.
questions.asked: It explains why coordinate and range tuples suddenly become arrays after a transformation.

questions.code:
function search(query: string, limit?: number) {}
type P = Parameters<typeof search>;
choices: `[query: string, limit?: number]`
`[string, number]`
`{ query: string; limit?: number }`
`(string | number | undefined)[]`
questions.why: `Parameters` returns a tuple that keeps the parameter names as labels and the optional marker, so the tuple accepts one or two elements. Labels are documentation only; they do not change assignability.
questions.asked: Wrapping functions (logging, retries, debounce) needs their parameter tuple, so reading this output matters.

questions.q: Which value is not assignable to `Line`?
questions.code: type Line = [sku: string, qty?: number];
choices: `['pen', undefined]`
questions.why: An optional tuple element may be omitted (or `undefined` without `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`), so the length is `1 | 2`. A third element exceeds the tuple, which would need a rest element such as `...number[]`.
questions.asked: Optional tuple elements appear in hook return types and function parameter lists.

questions.q: Which value can be assigned to `Record<string, never>`?
choices: `{ id: 1 }`, since `never` accepts anything
`{}`, an object with no properties
`{ id: undefined }`, since it is missing
`null`, the only value of type `never`
questions.why: Every property would have to be `never`, which no value is, so only an object with no properties fits. It is a common way to type "an empty object", since `{}` itself accepts almost anything non-nullish.
questions.asked: Typing empty props or empty config objects is common, and `{}` is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: What is the type of `email` in `Verified`?
questions.code:
type User = { id: string; email?: string };
type Verified = User & Required<Pick<User, 'email'>>;
choices: `string | undefined`, as the left side wins
`string | undefined`, as `Required` is shallow
`never`, as the two declarations conflict
`string`, as the intersection makes it required
questions.why: Intersecting an optional property with a required one of the same type yields a required property. This "make some keys required" idiom is common for states such as a user after email verification.
questions.asked: Adjusting one field's optionality without redefining a type comes up in almost every codebase.

choices: `'items' | 'add'`
`'items'`, since methods are not keys
`'items' | 'add' | 'length'`
`string`, since interfaces are open
questions.why: Methods are properties whose values are functions, so their names are part of `keyof`. To keep only data fields, filter with a mapped type that drops function-valued keys.
questions.asked: It sets up the follow-up question of how to get only the data keys of a model.

questions.q: Which value is not assignable to `Row`?
questions.code: type Row = [id: string, ...scores: number[]];
questions.why: A rest element allows any number of trailing elements of its type, including none, but the leading element must be a string. So `[1, 'a']` fails on both positions.
questions.asked: Rest tuples type variadic arguments, which is how `Parameters` and `...args` wrappers are modelled.

choices: `'id' | 'balance' | 'deposit'`
`'id' | 'balance' | '#pin' | 'deposit'`
`'id' | 'deposit'`
questions.why: `keyof` on a class instance type only includes public members; `private`, `protected` and `#private` members are excluded, even though a TS-private field exists as a normal property at runtime.
questions.asked: It clarifies what generic helpers like `pick(obj, key)` can reach on class instances.

choices: The type of the module's exports, with no runtime import
The runtime module object, loaded synchronously at that point
The type of the default export only
A string literal of the resolved file path
questions.why: An import type refers to a module's shape in a type position without adding an import statement, so there is no runtime cost or circular-load risk. It is often used in JSDoc and in `.d.ts` files.
questions.asked: It helps when typing lazy imports and when reading generated declaration files.

questions.q: A recursive type like `Path<T>` over a large API type reports "Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite". What is the usual fix?
choices: Turn off `strict` for the file that uses the type
Increase the compiler's stack size with a flag
Replace every `extends` with an `as` assertion
Bound the recursion, e.g. with a depth counter tuple
questions.why: The checker caps instantiation depth to stay fast; deep or unbounded recursion hits it. Limiting depth (a counter tuple that grows each step), simplifying the type, or giving up on full precision are the practical fixes; there is no flag to raise the limit.
questions.asked: Type-level code that slows the editor or hits limits is a real cost, and knowing when to stop is a senior trait.

questions.q: What does `satisfies` check in this code?
choices: That every action type has a handler, so `clear` is reported
Nothing, since `satisfies` is erased before checking
Only that each handler that exists is a function type
That `handlers` is readonly, like `as const` would
questions.why: `Record<Action['type'], ...>` requires all three keys, so the missing `clear` is an error, and adding an action later breaks this line. Unlike an annotation, `satisfies` keeps the object's own inferred type.
questions.asked: Exhaustive handler maps are a lightweight alternative to switch statements, and this is how they stay exhaustive.

questions.code:
type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never;
type E = ElementOf<readonly string[]>;
choices: `string`
`readonly string`
`never`
`unknown`
questions.why: A readonly array is not assignable to a mutable array pattern, so the conditional takes the false branch. Match `readonly (infer U)[]` instead, which accepts both mutable and readonly arrays.
questions.asked: Helpers that break on `as const` arrays are a common bug in hand-written utility types.

questions.q: A `.d.ts` file declares `function slugify(s: string): string;` and `namespace slugify { const separator: string; }`. What does this model?
choices: A conflict that tsc reports as a duplicate identifier
A function that also has a `separator` property
Two exports, `slugify` and `slugify.separator` as a file
An overload that takes a `separator` argument
questions.why: Functions and namespaces with the same name merge, which is how declaration files describe JS functions that carry properties. In your own code you would usually write a function with an assigned property instead.
questions.asked: Reading third-party `.d.ts` files is a senior expectation, and merging is one of their idioms.

questions.q: Which declaration types `process.env.DATABASE_URL` as `string` across a Node project?
choices: `declare const process: { env: { DATABASE_URL: string } };`
`interface Env extends NodeJS.ProcessEnv { DATABASE_URL: string }` in a module
`type ProcessEnv = { DATABASE_URL: string };` in a `.d.ts` file
`declare global { namespace NodeJS { interface ProcessEnv { DATABASE_URL: string } } }`
questions.why: `@types/node` declares `process.env` as `NodeJS.ProcessEnv`, so merging a property into that interface changes every read. It is only a claim, though: validate env at startup so the type is true.
questions.asked: Env typing is a common setup task, and a good answer adds that validation must back the type.

choices: `undefined`
`unknown`
`never[] | undefined`
`any`
questions.why: With an empty array literal, `T` is inferred as `never`, and `never | undefined` simplifies to `undefined`. Passing a typed array, or `first<User>([])`, gives the intended result.
questions.asked: It shows how inference behaves with empty inputs, a common source of surprising `never` types.

questions.q: Why do linters flag a parameter typed `Function`?
choices: `Function` only accepts class constructors
`Function` excludes arrow functions
`Function` values cannot be called without `.apply`
Calls on `Function` are unchecked and return `any`
questions.why: Any function is assignable to `Function`, and calling it accepts any arguments and returns `any`, so types are lost on both sides. Use a specific signature, e.g. `<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>) => Promise<T>`.
questions.asked: It is a common review comment, and the generic replacement is a good small exercise.

choices: `UserRepo`
`typeof UserRepo`
`object`
An error: classes cannot be passed
questions.why: A construct signature `new () => T` describes a class value; passing `UserRepo` infers `T` as its instance type. This is how DI containers and test factories are typed.
questions.asked: Factories that take a class are common in DI and testing, and construct signatures are how you type them.

questions.q: Why does tsc reject these overloads?
choices: Every overload must return the same type as the rest
Overloads need the `overload` keyword
Implementations must declare a return type
The implementation cannot accept a `number`
questions.why: Each overload must be compatible with the implementation signature, which is hidden from callers. Here the second overload promises to accept a number, but the implementation only takes strings; widen it to `x: string | number` and handle both.
questions.asked: Writing overloads correctly comes up when typing utility functions and reading library code.

choices: `a`, since intrinsic types need literal inputs
`b`, since it contains uppercase letters
`c`, since digits are not lowercase characters
None, since `Lowercase<string>` is just `string`
questions.why: Applied to `string`, the intrinsic string types produce pattern types, so `Lowercase<string>` accepts only strings unchanged by lowercasing. Digits and hyphens are unaffected, so `c` passes.
questions.asked: It shows familiarity with pattern template types, used for typed slugs, IDs and header names.

questions.code:
type Getter<T> = T extends { get(): infer R } ? R : never;
type R = Getter<{ get(): Promise<number>; set(v: number): void }>;
choices: `Promise<number>`
`number`, unwrapped from the promise
`() => Promise<number>`, the method
`never`, as `set` breaks the match
questions.why: `infer` can capture any position in a structural pattern, here the return type of a method. The extra `set` member does not stop the match, since the pattern only needs `get`. Unwrapping the promise would need `Awaited`.
questions.asked: Pattern-matching with `infer` is how many library helper types work, so reading one quickly is expected.

questions.q: What do these call signatures give an event emitter?
choices: Two properties named `on` that override each other
An error, since interfaces cannot declare overloads
A single `on` whose callback takes `string | number`
Overloads: the callback type follows the event name
